question: Inherited hyperammonemia is a result of deficiency of which enzyme of Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "N-acetyl glutamate synthetase deficiency" -> "decreased N-acetylglutamate" -> "reduced activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I" -> "impaired urea cycle" -> "accumulation of ammonia" -> "hyperammonemia" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Malate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Isocitrate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
CHAIN: "Succinate dehydrogenase deficiency" -> "impaired Krebs cycle" -> "possible metabolic disturbances" -> "unclear link to hyperammonemia" -> 20%
analysis: Inherited hyperammonemia is primarily associated with deficiencies in enzymes of the urea cycle, not the Krebs cycle. The urea cycle is responsible for converting ammonia into urea, which is then excreted from the body. A deficiency in N-acetyl glutamate synthetase leads to decreased production of N-acetylglutamate, an essential activator of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I, the first enzyme in the urea cycle. This deficiency impairs the urea cycle, resulting in the accumulation of ammonia and causing hyperammonemia. The other options listed (malate dehydrogenase, isocitrate dehydrogenase, and succinate dehydrogenase) are enzymes of the Krebs cycle and are not directly involved in the urea cycle or the regulation of ammonia levels. Therefore, the most likely correct answer, based on standard medical knowledge and consensus, is N-acetyl glutamate synthetase deficiency.
